candidates.label: Sebastia
candidates.support: Pleiades' point for the city of Samaria, also called Sebaste, is corroborated by the Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire's independently recorded point for the same site, about 100 meters away, at the modern village of Sebastiya.

summary.text: Samaria was the capital of the former northern kingdom of Israel, founded by King Omri on a hill he purchased. Herod the Great rebuilt and greatly enlarged the city, renaming it Sebaste, the Greek equivalent of "Augusta," in honor of the emperor Augustus. Acts describes Philip the evangelist proclaiming Christ in "the city of Samaria," with many believing and being baptized. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it is commonly thought this city was the scene of Philip's preaching, "but the absence of the definite article in Ac 8:5 makes this doubtful."

history.text: The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records that John Hyrcanus took the city after a year's siege in 120 BC and tried to destroy it utterly; it was rebuilt by the Roman general Pompey and, having again fallen under misfortune, was restored by Gabinius, before Herod the Great's far larger building program gave it the splendor evident in its later ruins, including a temple dedicated to Augustus and a great colonnaded street.
The same encyclopedia records that Herod had his wife Mariamne, and later his sons, put to death at Samaria.

scripture.textWEB: Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.

otConnections.note: King Omri of Israel purchases the hill of Samaria and builds the city that becomes the Northern Kingdom's capital.
The Assyrian king besieges Samaria, which falls after three years, ending the Northern Kingdom.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
